description.short: The fourth of Wuyishan's 'Four Great Bushes', offering a mellow, sweet, and floral-fruity bouquet
description.overview: One of the legendary 'Four Great Famous Bushes' (Si Da Ming Cong) of the Wuyi Mountains, famous for its juicy sweetness and an extraordinary historical dispute sparked when a flash flood washed the mother bush down the mountain into a neighboring monastery's ravine.
description.leaf: Dark brown, medium-sized twisted leaves with distinct venation resembling a turtle shell
description.liquor: Bright amber-yellow, clear and lustrous infusion
description.aroma: Floral, subtly fruity, interwoven with delicate roasted tones and mineral undertones
description.taste: Smooth, naturally sweet, less aggressively roasted and mineral than Da Hong Pao, highlighting charming floral sweetness
description.processing: Standard Yancha craftsmanship: withering → tossing/bruising → fixation (kill-green) → strip rolling → medium-intensity traditional charcoal roasting

history.origin: According to mountain lore, a torrential rainstorm washed the original tea bush off a cliff in Niulankeng down into the territory of a neighboring temple, where monks nurtured it—giving rise to the 'water' aspect in its name.
history.development: A famous legal dispute erupted during the Qing dynasty between the two Buddhist temples over rightful ownership of the lucrative bush, eventually requiring local magistrates to adjudicate the harvest rights.
history.modern: Today, Shui Jin Gui is propagated through vegetative cuttings across select protected valleys in Wuyishan to preserve its unique heritage.
interestingFacts: It is the only member of the 'Four Great Famous Bushes' whose historical acclaim stems not from an emperor's decree, but from a dramatic monastery lawsuit over property rights.
The name translates to 'Golden Water Turtle'—referencing the glossy leaves with raised veins that closely resemble the shell pattern of a swimming turtle.
